title: Cited research and AI insights built into provision and direct-tax workflows
problem: After the books close, tax teams face immediate pressure to finish the provision, and research interruptions slow the work.
approach: Bloomberg Tax places AI insights and rates inside Workpapers spreadsheets; Thomson Reuters embedded CoCounsel Tax in ONESOURCE direct tax in late 2024.
Thomson Reuters says research that took hours now takes minutes (vendor-published); neither source names a customer.
The preparer reads the linked primary sources before relying on an answer.

title: Idea: AI analysis of Excel-based provision workpapers
problem: This is an idea: many provision teams still build workpapers in Excel, which vendor Finrep calls a control risk auditors are increasingly unwilling to accept.
approach: An AI assistant would read provision workbooks to explain formulas, check tie-outs and answer questions.
A 2026 Tax Executives Institute programme scheduled an AI-for-Excel lab; no provision team is shown doing this.
No source describes the review step.

title: Provision data assembly and the close-to-tax handoff
problem: The provision runs on close data, and vendor Kognitos calls the handoff from close to tax a manual, error-prone junction where accuracy is decided.
approach: Bloomberg Tax describes automated data cleansing, rollforwards and book-to-tax adjustments in Workpapers that push into Provision.
Thomson Reuters aims for agentic data import, validation and mapping; Kognitos describes an upstream agent layer that reconciles ledger data.
No source says who reviews exceptions; direct tax professionals keep oversight of import, validation and mapping.

title: Pre-close anomaly flagging and document comparison in provision review
problem: Reviewers must catch outliers in deferred tax balances, rate reconciliation lines and source documents before the provision is final.
approach: Finrep describes comparing deferred tax balances with historical patterns and flagging outliers; CSC Corptax lists PDF comparison on its AI roadmap.
Thomson Reuters advertised for a specialist to build anomaly detection into ONESOURCE Tax Provision; these are development signals, not shipped features.
Flagged outliers go to human review before close.

title: Assembling the rate reconciliation and taxes-paid disclosure under the new accounting standard
problem: ASU 2023-09 requires public entities to give a detailed tabular rate reconciliation and split income taxes paid by federal, state and foreign jurisdiction.
approach: Finrep says AI-assisted categorisation of reconciling items from ERP data is the answer; vendor pages do not confirm this.
Neither vendor's own page was found to confirm this; no outcome figures are published (vendor-published).
The tax director reviews and approves the categorisation and the narrative.

title: Idea: generative AI first draft of income tax footnote disclosures
problem: This is an idea: tax disclosures must be company-specific and consistent with the provision, and Finrep says generic AI language risks SEC comment letters.
approach: Generative AI would draft disclosure language from provision data; Finrep says Big Four firms are piloting this, without a source.
The PCAOB found preparers using generative AI for first drafts of internal documents, not specifically tax disclosures.
A tax professional reviews, edits and approves every draft.

title: Live R&D credit data feeding provision estimates
problem: R&D credit amounts in the provision can rest on estimates or prior-year placeholders rather than live data, and revised Form 6765 adds business-component reporting.
approach: Thomson Reuters says Neo.Tax links project tools, groups data into components, applies the four-part test and allocates costs.
Thomson Reuters says live data makes the credit visible in real time and can reduce return-to-provision adjustments; no figures (vendor-published).
No source describes the review step.

title: Law-change monitoring feeding the provision and Pillar Two compliance
problem: Enacted-law changes drive deferred tax remeasurement, and Pillar Two rules keep moving, with new OECD packages in January and September 2026.
approach: Orbitax's Tax Flows mode tracks regulatory changes and sends comparison reports; CSC Corptax lists tax code version tracking on its roadmap.
KPMG US's tax vice chair says building an agent for changing tax rules went from weeks to minutes (self-reported).
No source describes the review step beyond reports going to stakeholders.

title: Pillar Two data collection seeded from validated country-by-country reporting data
problem: Pillar Two data drives actual tax and needs more granular data than finance and country-by-country reporting held; the first return needed over 100 data points.
approach: AMG Critical Materials loaded validated reporting XML into Orbitax's Accelerator, then added extra data; sources describe software automation, not AI.
Orbitax's case study says AMG's path to implementation shortened to around 10 days (vendor-published).
The tax team completes and reviews the additional information; AMG says it kept control of the financial data.

title: Idea: AI-assisted mapping of ERP data to global minimum tax data points
problem: This is an idea: Pillar Two needs jurisdiction-level calculations built from entity data held in several ERP systems, a substantial change from single-entity income tax work.
approach: EY's technology leader says AI can assist in mapping ERP data to common standards, but standardisation is long-term and needs governance.
Intrinsic data-quality issues still need human correction; flagged data issues get manual review and correction.

title: Pillar Two computation with safe-harbour tests, scenarios and interim estimates
problem: Global minimum tax calculations must be run by jurisdiction while the rules keep changing, including new safe harbours and a revised information return in 2026.
approach: EY's GloBE Engine and Deloitte's Pillar Two Agent hold the rules and run compliance and scenarios; sources call them rules-based, not AI.
A Swiss-parented insurer ran Orbitax as an independent check on its Excel calculations, surfacing data issues before filing (vendor-published).
The team reviews dashboards and reports before filing, and in-scope groups must assess the safe-harbour components themselves.

title: Pillar Two return population, XML generation, validation and direct filing
problem: For many groups the first return season was an XML problem more than a tax-law problem, with country schema variants, early portal gatekeeping and errors in the OECD schema.
approach: Platforms populate the return, generate and validate XML, and file by machine link where allowed; sources describe rules-based tooling, not AI.
Orbitax says it prepared or submitted more than 1,700 Pillar Two filings across 34 jurisdictions (vendor-published).
The tax team reviews validation results and resolves errors, which an insurer called the most demanding part of the season.

title: Correction and amendment management for Pillar Two returns
problem: Corrections to the Pillar Two return work only against accepted messages and need reference tracking; more corrections are expected as rules change.
approach: Law firm FGS says its Pillar 2 Management App supports correction returns and largely automates correction references; rules-based, no AI claimed.
FGS names no client and publishes no figures (vendor-published).
No source describes the review step.

title: Conversational assistant over live Pillar Two scenarios
problem: After calculations are done, the remaining work is reviewing data, answering finance and audit-committee questions, validating XML and documenting decisions.
approach: Orbitax says its XatBot assistant reads live scenarios, answers questions in plain language, analyses uploaded files and drafts audit-committee updates.
In Autopilot mode it can create and navigate scenarios from a conversation; no outcome figures are published (vendor-published).
The user can review the generated workflow before it runs, and professional judgment applies to anything entering a filing.

title: Firm-run Pillar Two platform with specialist team, sold as co-sourcing
problem: Heads of Tax must run Pillar Two compliance quickly with audit-ready transparency; 70% of surveyed leaders expect to pay over US$500,000 a year to comply.
approach: Deloitte offers its Pillar Two Agent only with its tax team, which collects data, calculates top-up tax and files; EY offers similar.
The sources do not describe AI, and no outcome figures are published (vendor-published).
The platform offers clients options for reviewing and signing off on data.

title: Bringing Pillar Two compliance in-house on a platform instead of outsourcing
problem: AMG's small tax function could not add headcount for Pillar Two and had to choose between outsourcing and building the capability itself.
approach: AMG chose software run in-house, as did a Swiss-parented insurer with a lean tax team; the sources describe software, not AI.
Orbitax says AMG's two-person tax function delivered first-year compliance across 70-80 entities in 25 jurisdictions with no added headcount (vendor-published).
AMG's vice president of tax reviewed and filed the returns.
